questions.skillExplanation: Q1 tests whether the learner can name a pictured container by integrating the sentence frame with the object shown, rather than guessing from familiar container words.
reasoningOperations: The illustration shows the man holding a basket containing grapes, so basket is the container noun that completes the sentence.
Compare the pictured container with the physical meanings of bag, bowl, and box rather than choosing by general plausibility.
questions.questionMechanism: The blank itself accepts several countable container nouns, so the picture must supply the discriminating feature that identifies basket.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: All four options can grammatically follow 'a,' but only basket matches the depicted grape container; the item therefore forces visual-semantic matching instead of grammar-only elimination.
questions.correctRationale: The picture shows a basket of grapes in the man's hands, matching option B.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Page 2 illustration for Q1 shows the man holding the grape container identified by the official answer as a basket.

A.rationale: A bag is a plausible grape container in real life, but it does not match the pictured container.
A.misconceptionTarget: Treating real-world possibility as sufficient without checking the visual evidence.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The illustrated container is not a bag.

C.rationale: A bowl could hold grapes, but the object in the source image is not a bowl.
C.misconceptionTarget: Ignoring the object's depicted shape and choosing any semantically compatible container.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The illustrated container does not have the appearance of a bowl.

D.rationale: A box is another possible container, but it conflicts with the container shown in the picture.
D.misconceptionTarget: Answering from generic container vocabulary rather than the required image.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The pictured grape container is not a box.

studentFailureModes: Reading only the sentence and ignoring that the instruction explicitly requires the picture.
Choosing any noun that could logically contain grapes without matching the visual form.
misconceptionsTargeted: Semantic possibility is the same as visual evidence.
A picture-based vocabulary item can be solved from the text alone.

shallowRecall.explanation: Once the visual object is recognized, the task is a direct noun-to-object mapping.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Use a syntactically permissive sentence frame with several real-world-plausible nouns, then let one clearly depicted physical feature determine the answer.
simplificationConstraints: Keep the picture indispensable and preserve four visually distinct container meanings.
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Add a second visual clue, such as how the container is carried, that must be integrated with its shape.
uncertainties: Direct pixel inspection was unavailable in this run; the analysis is grounded in the committed asset requirement, extraction metadata, and locked official answer.

questions.skillExplanation: Q2 asks the learner to infer the activity from the causal clue 'beautiful voice' and select the verb whose meaning depends on vocal performance.
reasoningOperations: Use the second sentence as a causal clue: pride in a beautiful voice explains why Dennis enjoys singing in public.
Reject activities that can occur in public but are not supported by the voice clue.
questions.questionMechanism: The first clause alone allows many public activities; the following sentence narrows the answer by explaining what personal ability Dennis is proud to display.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: Dancing, drawing, and shopping are all ordinary public activities, so the item only becomes determinate when the learner connects 'beautiful voice' to singing.
questions.correctRationale: A beautiful voice is directly relevant to singing, making D the only option explained by the second sentence.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Dennis enjoys _____ in public. He is proud of his beautiful voice.

A.rationale: Dancing can be performed in public, but the clue about a beautiful voice does not explain dancing.
A.misconceptionTarget: Using only the first sentence and ignoring the explanatory second sentence.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The decisive clue is 'beautiful voice,' which does not support dancing.

B.rationale: Drawing is compatible with 'enjoys ... in public' but has no semantic connection to vocal ability.
B.misconceptionTarget: Accepting grammatical fit without checking semantic cohesion across the sentence pair.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The voice clue gives no support for drawing.

C.rationale: Shopping can happen in public, yet a beautiful voice does not motivate or characterize shopping.
C.misconceptionTarget: Choosing a common public activity while overlooking the causal clue.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The second sentence explains the activity through Dennis's voice, excluding shopping.

studentFailureModes: Stopping after finding an option that sounds natural after 'enjoys.'
Failing to treat the second sentence as evidence that constrains the blank.
misconceptionsTargeted: Grammatical compatibility is enough for a vocabulary-in-context answer.
Adjacent explanatory sentences do not need to be integrated.

shallowRecall.explanation: The learner must connect the activity to a clue in the next sentence, not merely recall a word definition.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Place several grammatically valid activity words in the options, then use a short follow-up sentence that uniquely explains one of them through a concrete ability or motive.
simplificationConstraints: Preserve the explanatory relationship between the activity and the clue about voice.
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Make the identifying ability implicit across two short clues instead of naming 'voice' directly.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: Dennis enjoys _____ in public. He is proud of his beautiful voice.

questions.skillExplanation: Q3 requires choosing an action that directly responds to the stated hearing difficulty, so the answer follows from a simple problem-to-remedy relation.
reasoningOperations: Identify the problem: Mrs. Johnson cannot hear well.
Choose the response that increases audibility; shouting is the only option that does so.
questions.questionMechanism: The first sentence establishes a sensory limitation and the conditional second sentence asks for a compensating action, turning the item into a cause-and-remedy vocabulary choice.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: Explain, hurry, and listen are all communication-related or action verbs, but only shout changes the loudness of the speaker's voice and therefore addresses poor hearing.
questions.correctRationale: If someone cannot hear well, speaking very loudly can help them hear; 'shout' is the only option with that effect.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Mrs. Johnson can’t hear very well. If you need to talk to her, you must _____ .

A.rationale: Explaining can make meaning clearer, but it does not make speech louder for a person who has difficulty hearing.
A.misconceptionTarget: Confusing clarity of explanation with physical audibility.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The stated problem is hearing, not understanding the explanation.

B.rationale: Hurrying changes the speed of an action and does nothing to make speech easier to hear.
B.misconceptionTarget: Selecting a general imperative verb without matching it to the diagnosed problem.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Poor hearing requires greater audibility, which hurrying does not provide.

C.rationale: Listening is an action for the hearer, while the blank asks what 'you' should do when speaking to Mrs. Johnson.
C.misconceptionTarget: Reversing the roles of speaker and listener.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The subject of the required action is 'you,' the person who needs to talk to Mrs. Johnson.

studentFailureModes: Choosing a communication-related verb without asking whether it solves the specific hearing problem.
Losing track of who performs the action in the conditional sentence.
misconceptionsTargeted: Any communication verb fits a communication situation.
The roles of speaker and listener can be ignored when interpreting the blank.

shallowRecall.explanation: The meaning of shout is easy, but selecting it requires applying the preceding problem statement to the action choice.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: State a concrete limitation first, then offer several semantically neighboring actions so that only one actually remedies the limitation.
simplificationConstraints: Keep the hearing problem explicit and preserve speaker/listener roles.
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Describe the hearing difficulty indirectly through behavior, requiring the learner to infer the limitation before selecting the remedy.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: Mrs. Johnson can’t hear very well. If you need to talk to her, you must _____ .

questions.skillExplanation: Q4 tests the perception-verb pattern watch + object + present participle, with the -ing form presenting an action observed in progress.
reasoningOperations: Identify watched as a perception verb followed by the object Ms. Smith.
Select dancing because watch + object can take a present participle to describe the observed action in progress.
questions.questionMechanism: All four choices are forms of dance, so lexical meaning cannot distinguish them; the learner must recognize the complement structure licensed by watched Ms. Smith.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: The distractors preserve the same lexical verb while varying tense and infinitival morphology, isolating knowledge of the perception-verb complement rather than vocabulary recall.
questions.correctRationale: In 'watched Ms. Smith dancing,' dancing functions as the participial complement describing what people observed Ms. Smith doing, so B fits the sentence.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: People got very excited when they watched Ms. Smith _____ at the party.

A.rationale: Danced is a finite past-tense form and cannot directly serve as the complement after the object in 'watched Ms. Smith ___.',
A.misconceptionTarget: Treating the blank as a new finite clause simply because the surrounding event is in the past.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The blank follows the object 'Ms. Smith' inside the complement of 'watched,' not an independent subject position.

C.rationale: Has danced is a finite perfect verb phrase and would require its own clause structure; it cannot follow 'watched Ms. Smith' in this pattern.
C.misconceptionTarget: Choosing a familiar completed-action tense without checking syntactic licensing.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The perception-verb construction does not license a finite present-perfect phrase after the object.

D.rationale: To dance is not the complement form used with watch in this active perception construction; English uses the bare infinitive or -ing form instead.
D.misconceptionTarget: Overgeneralizing the common verb + object + to-infinitive pattern to perception verbs.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: After active 'watch + object,' a to-infinitive is not licensed here.

studentFailureModes: Matching the past tense of watched with danced by surface agreement.
Assuming every verb followed by an object takes a to-infinitive complement.
misconceptionsTargeted: Past-time context requires every verb form in the sentence to be past tense.
Perception verbs follow the same complement pattern as ask/tell/want.

shallowRecall.explanation: The item requires applying a syntactic complement pattern to the exact position of the blank.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Hold lexical meaning constant across options and vary only verb morphology to isolate whether learners understand a high-value complement pattern.
simplificationConstraints: Keep watch + person + blank and retain competing finite, -ing, and to-infinitive forms.
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Contrast bare infinitive versus -ing in a context where event completeness determines which interpretation is more natural.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: Official 112 CAP item: People got very excited when they watched Ms. Smith _____ at the party.

questions.skillExplanation: Q5 requires using the later clue 'the white pair looked best' to infer that the shoes were tried in different colors.
reasoningOperations: Notice that 'white pair' identifies a color category.
Choose colors because the comparison being reported is which appearance looked best, while price, shape, and size do not explain the adjective white.
questions.questionMechanism: The first clause permits several dimensions along which shoes can differ, but the post-blank clue 'white pair' retroactively identifies the intended dimension as color.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: Prices, shapes, and sizes are all realistic attributes of shoes, making them locally plausible until the learner integrates the decisive color adjective later in the sentence.
questions.correctRationale: White names a color, so trying the shoes in several different colors is the only choice that makes the comparison coherent; A is correct.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: I tried on these shoes in several different _____, and I thought the white pair looked best on me.

B.rationale: Shoes can have different prices, but describing one pair as white does not identify its price.
B.misconceptionTarget: Choosing a realistic shoe attribute without integrating the later clue.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: 'White pair' categorizes appearance by color, not cost.

C.rationale: Shoes can differ in shape, yet white does not describe shape.
C.misconceptionTarget: Stopping at general semantic plausibility rather than matching the comparison dimension.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The explicit adjective 'white' points to color rather than shape.

D.rationale: Trying shoes in different sizes is common, but a 'white pair' is not a size label and 'looked best on me' focuses appearance rather than fit.
D.misconceptionTarget: Relying on a familiar shopping script instead of the sentence's lexical evidence.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The distinguishing label supplied by the sentence is 'white.'

studentFailureModes: Selecting sizes because trying on shoe sizes is a familiar real-world action.
Answering before reading the clause after the comma.
misconceptionsTargeted: Real-world frequency outweighs explicit textual evidence.
A blank can be solved safely without integrating later context in the same sentence.

shallowRecall.explanation: All option meanings are common; the challenge is using the later adjective as a semantic discriminator.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Offer several realistic attributes of the same object, then place a post-blank clue that names an instance of exactly one attribute category.
simplificationConstraints: Keep a concrete example such as 'white pair' after the blank so backward integration remains necessary.
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Replace the direct color label with two appearance clues that jointly imply the relevant comparison dimension.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: Official 112 CAP item contrasts several shoe attributes and identifies the preferred pair as white.

questions.skillExplanation: Q6 tests whether the learner can use the past progressive for an action already in progress at the specific past time when the earthquake occurred.
reasoningOperations: Anchor the situation to the completed past event 'the earthquake this morning.'
Use 'at the time' to identify a simultaneous ongoing action, requiring was jogging.
questions.questionMechanism: The lexical verb is held constant while tense/aspect changes; 'at the time' forces the learner to represent jogging as ongoing during a past reference point.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: Simple past, present perfect, and conditional-like would forms are morphologically familiar, but only past progressive correctly encodes simultaneity with the earthquake's past moment.
questions.correctRationale: The earthquake provides a past reference time and Rex's jogging was in progress then, so 'was jogging' is the appropriate past progressive form, B.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Rex did not feel the earthquake this morning. He _____ in the park at the time.

A.rationale: Jogged places the action in the past but does not express that it was ongoing at the earthquake's reference moment.
A.misconceptionTarget: Using simple past for every completed past-time context without considering aspect.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: 'At the time' highlights an action in progress at a specific past point.

C.rationale: Has jogged links a past action to the present and conflicts with the explicitly located past reference time 'this morning ... at the time.'
C.misconceptionTarget: Choosing present perfect whenever an action occurred before now.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The sentence supplies a definite past event as the reference point.

D.rationale: Would jog normally needs a past-future, habitual, or conditional frame that the sentence does not provide.
D.misconceptionTarget: Treating would + verb as a generic alternative past form.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: No condition, past-future viewpoint, or repeated-habit cue licenses 'would jog.'

studentFailureModes: Seeing 'this morning' and choosing simple past without processing 'at the time.'
Knowing tense labels but not mapping past progressive to an action in progress at another past event.
misconceptionsTargeted: Any action in a past story should use simple past.
Present perfect can be used with any event that happened earlier today regardless of a definite past reference point.

shallowRecall.explanation: The learner must map temporal relations between two events onto aspect, not simply recall a conjugation.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Pair a punctual past event with 'at the time' and vary only tense/aspect forms of one verb to test temporal representation cleanly.
simplificationConstraints: Preserve a clear past reference event and a simultaneity cue such as 'at the time.'
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Remove 'at the time' and make simultaneity inferable from the causal relation between the two events.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: Official 112 CAP item: Rex did not feel the earthquake this morning. He _____ in the park at the time.
